title: QMA versus \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)=\mathrm{QMA}\) for ordinary uniform promise problems without an oracle? A QMA(2) verifier receives two polynomial-length quantum witnesses that are promised to be unentangled across the two witness registers, even on a no-instance. A QMA verifier receives one arbitrary polynomial-length quantum witness. The easy inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) follows by ignoring a second witness; the question is whether every QMA(2) promise problem is also in QMA under the definitions below.
why: This asks whether a promise of independence between two untrusted quantum messages can increase what an efficient quantum computer can verify. It connects computational verification with the geometry of entanglement and separates the value of unentanglement from simply supplying more qubits.
status_note: Source-open for the ordinary QMA versus QMA(2) comparison. On 16 September 2026 the full ITCS 2024 source, Harrow–Montanaro’s primary abstract, and the 2 September 2026 oracle manuscript’s introduction, Theorem 1.1 and model distinctions were checked. The latest manuscript updates the quantum-oracle status but explicitly retains the ordinary-class question. A bounded later-work search identified no unrelativized resolution. Cited proofs, including the new preprint, were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

progress.text: Harrow–Montanaro obtain amplification and equivalence between two and polynomially many unentangled witnesses.
Bassirian–Fefferman–Marwaha separate the effects of phase restrictions from ordinary QMA(2), and explicitly retain the latter’s relationship to QMA as an open question.

Bostanci and coauthors post a unitary-oracle separation between QMA(2) and QMA. Their introduction retains the ordinary-class question and their footnote distinguishes the still-open classical-oracle case.

importance.reason: A central unresolved comparison in quantum proof complexity, connecting unentanglement, separable optimization and verification. The unusually broad known containment range and the new oracle separation make its ordinary-class target substantial; the score is for equality of QMA and QMA(2), not an unrestricted request to classify every multiprover model.

sentences: QMA(2) receives two quantum witnesses that are promised unentangled across a specified division, whereas QMA receives one unrestricted quantum witness.
Both use uniform polynomial-time quantum verification with constant completeness and soundness error.
The question is whether the promise of unentanglement adds power for ordinary promise problems without an oracle.
Known amplification and restricted-phase results do not resolve this comparison, and concatenating honest witnesses does not preserve soundness automatically.
A September 2026 manuscript separates the classes relative to a unitary oracle while explicitly leaving their ordinary relationship unresolved.

definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), the verifier instead has two witness registers, each of length bounded by a polynomial in the input length. For every yes-input there must exist density matrices \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\) on the respective registers such that the product state \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\). For every no-input and every pair \(\rho,\sigma\), the acceptance probability on \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is at most \(1/3\). The two factors can each have arbitrary internal entanglement among their own qubits; the restriction concerns the division between the two registers. Equivalent soundness quantification allows every separable state \(\sum_jp_j\rho_j\otimes\sigma_j\), where \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\), because acceptance is linear. The two witnesses need not be identical. Both may depend on the whole input and may be coordinated before they are sent, but their joint state at receipt must satisfy the indicated separability restriction. After receipt, the verifier may perform arbitrary allowed joint gates and create entanglement. It is not required to test separability of an arbitrary incoming state; separability is a promise on the states against which soundness is required. Neither class restricts amplitudes to be nonnegative or witness states to have short classical descriptions. Equality means equality of all disjoint promise pairs admitted by the two definitions.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some promise problem lies in QMA(2) but outside QMA. An equality proof must supply sound single-witness verification for every eligible two-witness problem; merely concatenating the intended honest witnesses is insufficient because the single-witness verifier must also resist entangled dishonest states. A separation must exclude every ordinary uniform polynomial-time QMA verifier for the same promise pair. A quantum- or classical-oracle separation, a result about a restricted-amplitude class, or a state-generation task does not alone settle this decision-class comparison.

source_formulation.text: Does the promise that two quantum witnesses are unentangled give more verification power than an unrestricted single quantum witness?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Section 6, Question 1

context_blocks.text: The two-witness condition changes which dishonest messages a verifier must handle. A verifier designed for a product state may be fooled by an entangled state on the same two registers. Treating both registers as one long witness preserves an honest proof but can invalidate soundness; this is why the class comparison is nontrivial.

There is no resource advantage just from having twice as many qubits: a single polynomial-length witness can already contain that many. Nor does the model provide two-way interaction or ask the verifier to certify that an arbitrary state is unentangled. The product-state restriction is part of the proof-system model.

The ordinary inclusions recorded in both the 2024 source and the September 2026 manuscript are \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\). Here NEXP is the class of promise problems decidable by a nondeterministic classical Turing machine in time \(2^{p(n)}\) for some polynomial \(p\), with an accepting branch on every yes-input and no accepting branch on any no-input. These inclusions alone neither prove nor refute equality of the first two classes.

Harrow–Montanaro establish error amplification and show that two unentangled proofs can simulate polynomially many. This explains why the two-proof class captures a broad finite-message regime, while still leaving comparison with one unrestricted quantum witness open.

The 2024 source studies witnesses whose relative phases are restricted, including nonnegative-amplitude variants at specified completeness and soundness parameters. It explicitly warns that those results do not immediately establish the relationship between ordinary QMA and QMA(2). A restriction on which dishonest states are allowed can increase verification power, so it cannot be transferred by treating it as an innocuous representation change.

The September 2026 manuscript gives the first separation relative to a unitary oracle. Both verifiers receive access to the same quantum black box, and the two-proof verifier gains power in that setting. This updates the 2024 paper’s statement that even such an oracle separation was unknown, but it does not separate the ordinary classes.

The new manuscript also draws consequences for approximate disentanglers and explicitly says a classical-oracle separation remains open. These are separate statements with their own parameters; neither is substituted for the unrelativized equality asked here. The recorded status is a manuscript claim checked for scope, not an independent validation of its proof.
